source_text: Post paucos dies rumor cucurrit ut audiremur. Superuenit autem et de ciuitate pater meus, consumptus taedio, et ascendit ad me, ut me deiceret, dicens: Filia, miserere canis meis; miserere patri, si dignus sum a te pater uocari; si his te manibus ad hunc florem aetatis prouexi, si te praeposui omnibus fratribus tuis: ne me dederis in dedecus hominum. Aspice fratres tuos, aspice matrem tuam et materteram, aspice filium tuum, qui post te uiuere non poterit. Depone animos; ne uniuersos nos extermines: nemo enim nostrum libere loquetur, si tu aliquid fueris passa. Haec dicebat quasi pater pro sua pietate, basians mihi manus, et se ad pedes meos iactans et lacrimans me iam non filiam nominabat, sed dominam. Et ego dolebam casum patris mei, quod solus de passione mea gauisurus non esset de toto genere meo; et confortaui eum dicens: Hoc fiet in illa catasta quod deus uoluerit; scito enim nos non in nostra potestate esse futuros, sed in dei. Et recessit a me contristatus.
orientation: Perpetua herself narrates in her prison diary how her father comes to turn her back before her hearing.
pass_a_gloss: After a few days a rumor ran that we were to be heard in court. But my father also came suddenly from the city, worn out with distress, and he came up to me to bring me down, saying: Daughter, pity my white hairs; pity your father, if I am worthy to be called father by you; if with these hands I have led you to this flower of your age, if I have placed you before all your brothers: do not hand me over into the disgrace of men. Look at your brothers, look at your mother and your mothers sister, look at your son, who will not be able to live after you. Put away your resolve; do not wipe us all out: for no one of us will speak freely, if you shall have suffered anything. He kept saying these things as a father out of his dutiful love, kissing my hands, and throwing himself at my feet and weeping he kept calling me now not daughter, but lady. And I kept grieving for the fall of my father, because alone out of all my kin he was not going to rejoice over my martyrdom; and I strengthened him saying: On that platform what God shall have willed will happen; for know that we are going to be not in our own power, but in that of God. And he went away from me saddened.

lemmas.gloss: to be given a judicial hearing

choices.english: that we were to be heard in court
choices.why: judicial hearing before authority, not general listening
rejected: that we would be listened to

choices.why: literal metonymy for old age kept as body part, not smoothed to old age
plural imperative keeps command to abandon high purpose, not mere calming
brief glossary fixes passio as faithful witness unto death

pass_b_english: A few days later rumor spread that we were to be heard in court. My father came from the city, worn out with distress, and climbed up to me to make me fall. He said: “Daughter, pity my white hairs. Pity your father, if I deserve to be called father by you. If these hands raised you to this flower of life, if I set you above all your brothers, do not hand me over to the disgrace of men. Look at your brothers, look at your mother and your aunt, look at your son, who will not be able to live after you. Put away your resolve. Do not destroy us all. None of us will speak freely if anything happens to you.” He spoke as a father, out of dutiful love, kissing my hands and throwing himself at my feet, and weeping he called me no longer daughter but lady. And I grieved over my father’s fall, that alone of all my kin would not rejoice over my martyrdom. And I strengthened him by saying, “What God wills will happen on that platform. Know that we shall not be in our own power, but in God’s.” And he left me in sorrow.
